---
title: "Exercises — Compartments"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer. A calculator with an exponential
key helps; $e^{-x}\approx 1-x+x^2/2$ is good enough for small $x$.

# Part 1 — Poisson loading

## E1. Droplets by hand

You load a droplet generator so that the mean is 0.2 cells per droplet. What fraction of all
droplets hold no cell, exactly one cell, and two or more? What fraction of the occupied
droplets are multiplets?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
$P(0)=e^{-\lambda}$, $P(1)=\lambda P(0)$, and "two or more" is what remains.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
$P(0)=e^{-0.2}=0.819$. $P(1)=0.2\times0.819=0.164$. Two or more: $1-0.819-0.164=0.017$.
Occupied droplets are $1-0.819=0.181$, so multiplets are $0.017/0.181\approx 9.7\%$ of them, so about 90% of occupied droplets are
singletons. About 82% of the droplets are empty.
:::

## E2. How many cells do I have to load?

You want about 5,000 singlet cells and your system makes droplets in large excess. Using the
numbers for $\lambda=0.1$ (9.05% of droplets hold exactly one cell), how many droplets must
receive cells, and how many cells in total pass into droplets?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Singlets are 9.05% of droplets, so you need 5,000 / 0.0905 ≈ 55,000 droplets. The mean is 0.1
cells per droplet, so about 5,500 cells in total enter, of which 5,000 are in singlets and the rest are in
multiplets (about 260 droplets with two or more cells, holding roughly 520 cells). Real systems
also lose cells before encapsulation, so the number to load is higher.
:::

## E3. Two draws

A bead-based droplet system loads cells at $\lambda_c=0.1$ and beads at $\lambda_b=0.3$ per
droplet, independently. What fraction of droplets hold exactly one cell and at least one bead?
Why might more than one bead still be a problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Multiply the two probabilities. For beads, "at least one" is $1-P(0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
One cell: 0.0905. At least one bead: $1-e^{-0.3}=0.259$. Product: 0.0905 × 0.259 ≈ 2.3% of droplets.
Droplets with two or more beads give one cell two barcodes, so its RNA is split over two
apparent cells, which inflates cell numbers and lowers per-cell depth.
:::

## E4. Reading a barnyard plot

In a human–mouse mixing experiment at 1:1, 2.4% of barcodes are clearly mixed-species. Estimate
the total doublet fraction. Then state what changes if the mix is 9 human to 1 mouse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A doublet is mixed-species only if the two cells differ in species. What is the chance of that at 1:1?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
At 1:1 a doublet is mixed half of the time, so the total is about 2 × 2.4% = 4.8%. At 9:1 the
chance that two cells differ in species is $2\times0.9\times0.1=0.18$, so only 18% of doublets
are visible and you must multiply the observed fraction by about 5.6 (and the number is small and noisy). A 1:1 mix is the
most efficient design for this reason.
:::

# Part 2 — Choosing and designing

## E5. Split-pool arithmetic

A three-round split-pool design uses 48 wells in each round. How many distinct barcodes are
there? You recover 20,000 cells. What fraction share a barcode with another cell? How many
rounds of 48 would be needed to bring that below 1%?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The fraction sharing a barcode is about $1-e^{-n/N}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
$48^3=110{,}592$. $\lambda=20{,}000/110{,}592=0.181$, so about $1-e^{-0.181}=16.5\%$ of cells share a barcode
(counting cells that have at least one partner by chance). With four rounds, $N=48^4=5.3$ million, so
$\lambda=0.0038$ and about 0.4%. Four rounds are enough.
:::

## E6. Why fix?

Your tissue is dissociated with a process that stresses cells, and you are worried that gene
expression changes while cells wait in the loading queue. Name two things fixation changes in
the design and one thing it costs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Fixation freezes the transcript profile at the moment of fixation, so waiting does not matter,
and it lets you collect many samples over time and process them together. It also lets the cell act
as its own compartment, so no droplet is needed. The cost is chemistry: crosslinks make RNA
harder to reverse-transcribe and reduce sensitivity per cell, and the permeabilisation step must
be tuned so that molecules stay in while enzymes get in.
:::

## E7. Two-stage loading

A two-stage design pre-indexes nuclei into 384 wells and then loads droplets at 10 nuclei per
droplet on average. What fraction of nuclei share a droplet with another nucleus of the same
index? How does the answer change if you use 96 indexes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Other nuclei in the droplet are Poisson with mean 10. Those with the same index are Poisson with mean $10/N_{index}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
With 384 indexes: $1-e^{-10/384}=2.6\%$. With 96 indexes: $1-e^{-10/96}=9.9\%$. Both stay manageable even
though the droplets are heavily overloaded: a one-stage droplet at the same load would
have almost all droplets as multiplets. The index is what turns overload into a manageable
collision rate.
:::

## E8. What went wrong?

A single-cell run returns a barcode-rank plot with no clear knee: reads fall off smoothly from
the first barcode to the last. Give two explanations and say which control or measurement
distinguishes them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A knee appears when cells hold much more RNA than empty droplets. What would blur that?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
(1) Heavy ambient RNA, for example from dead cells in the suspension, so empty droplets have nearly as many reads as cells; check cell viability and the fraction of reads in mitochondrial genes. (2) A sample with a very wide range of cell
sizes or RNA content, so no clean separation exists; compare the profiles of low-count barcodes
with those of cells. A species-mix control would show how many reads of the other species
sit in each barcode, which measures the ambient fraction directly.
:::

# Self-check

1. What is the one thing that a compartment must keep attached to a molecule?
2. What is $P(0)$ at $\lambda=0.1$, and what does it say about cost?
3. Why does a species-mixing experiment under-count doublets?
4. In split-pool, what takes the place of the droplet?
5. How does two-stage encapsulation make overloaded droplets usable?
6. Why does a nucleus keep nascent RNA but lose cytoplasmic RNA?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. A barcode that names the compartment, written into the molecule.
2. $e^{-0.1}=0.905$: about 90% of droplets are empty, so most reagent volume is spent on nothing.
3. Doublets of two cells of the same species look like one cell.
4. The cell itself, fixed and permeabilised, with a barcode path built over several rounds.
5. A first-stage index makes cells in one droplet distinguishable, so only same-index collisions are a problem.
6. The nuclear membrane keeps what is inside the nucleus; cytoplasm is removed when the cell is lysed.
:::
